claims.text: Hf substitution changes local bonding, interatomic distances, and electronic environments in rare-earth-free Fe–Zr–B–Cu alloys.
These Hf-induced structural and electronic changes modulate the strength and range of magnetic exchange interactions.
Tuning magnetic exchange interactions through Hf substitution promotes a broadened, continuous second-order magnetic transition.
Fe88Zr3Hf4B4Cu1 and Fe88Zr1Hf6B4Cu1 undergo near-room-temperature second-order paramagnetic-to-ferromagnetic transitions.
A broadened second-order transition enhances the low-field magnetocaloric response.
Hf-containing Fe–Zr–B–Cu alloys exhibit enhanced magnetocaloric performance under a 2.5 T field change.
The broadened second-order transition minimizes magnetic hysteresis losses.
The proposed Hf tuning permits rapid heat exchange.
The proposed Hf tuning preserves mechanical stability or mechanical performance.
The baseline Fe–Zr–B–Cu alloy is a single-phase high-entropy alloy with a well-ordered microstructure.
The baseline Fe–Zr–B–Cu alloy has a moderate magnetocaloric effect and standard hysteresis characteristics.
Increasing Hf within approximately 3–7 at.% while otherwise holding composition constant is a controlled intervention for testing the hypothesis.
Hf substitution causes lattice distortion and microstructural heterogeneity without inducing a martensitic phase change.
An optimal Hf concentration will produce a marked increase in magnetic entropy change relative to a minimal-Hf baseline.
At the optimal Hf concentration, hysteresis will decrease relative to the baseline.
Too little or too much Hf will reduce magnetocaloric efficiency or increase hysteresis.
The hypothesis should apply only while the alloys remain single-phase, mechanically robust, and near a room-temperature second-order transition.
A lack of improved magnetic entropy change, or the occurrence of substantially increased hysteresis or mechanical degradation upon Hf addition, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
